title: Anyscale Pricing: Plans and Instance Costs (2026)
summary: Anyscale pricing is based on compute usage rather than fixed plans. See what you'll actually pay for different workloads and scale levels.
body_markdown:
## Undisclosed Anyscale costs and limits


Look past the rate card and you find a second bill from your cloud provider, head-node time, data egress, storage, GPU quotas and support access.


- Separate cloud-provider bill
- Idle and head-node time
- Autoscaling over-provisioning
- Egress
- Storage
- GPU quotas
- Support-tier gating


When clusters run in your own cloud account, the cloud provider invoices the virtual machines, disks and network, not Anyscale. Your finance team sees two invoices, and **the Anyscale one's the smaller story** .


While a cluster exists, the head node must stay up, so a cluster left waiting between jobs still bills for it. Autoscaling adds a second leak: workers added for a burst keep billing until the idle timeout releases them.


[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) can sit beside Anyscale for that nightly batch: a flow calls Anyscale's API or a webhook to start the job, then posts the spend or failure notice to Slack. Its meter is the run, not the steps inside it.


A run is 1 credit whether the flow has two steps or ten, and the Free plan carries 1,000 credits a month with unlimited flows.


Splitting the start, the status check and the notice into separate steps therefore costs nothing extra, which is why the routine around the cluster never changes the Anyscale meter.


### Anyscale quotas, data egress and storage fees


Pulling 5 TB of results to an outside system costs about $450 before any compute, so data egress is a budget line item that must be carefully planned.


The reason is the egress rate: data leaving AWS to the internet costs[$0.09 per GB for the first 10 TB](https://venvtech.com/en/company/blog/aws-data-transfer-costs-guide) , meaning even modest data pulls incur meaningful egress charges.


Past that first 10 TB, the rate falls to $0.085 per GB for the next 40 TB, $0.07 for the next 100 TB and $0.05 beyond 150 TB.


Volume discounts only reach teams already moving very large datasets, so small teams should budget at the top rate.


Whether or not a job runs, stored checkpoints and datasets bill monthly. GPU capacity's capped by your provider quota, and a quota increase request can take time, so a launch that needs 64 GPUs may wait on an approval.


When a cluster fails at 2 a.m., a team on a lower tier running production jobs has no contractual response time. Support response commitments and SLAs sit on the higher tiers, so the real price of that tier includes the outage risk.
